passage: I'm Rajni, and I sat behind a little boy called Nitin on the bus to town. He looked out of the window and asked his mother, "Why is the sky blue? Why is that cow brown? Why does the road go on?" She didn't know the sky one. She said, "Good question. I'll ask your uncle, he studied science." About the cow she said, "That's how she was born." Nitin nodded, satisfied, and asked the next one. I couldn't tell how much he understood, but he kept asking, and she kept turning to listen.

qa.q: What three questions did Nitin ask on the bus?
qa.a: Nitin asked why the sky is blue, why that cow is brown and why the road goes on.

qa.q: What was Nitin probably feeling as he kept asking?
qa.a: Nitin seemed curious and content, nodding when answered and moving on to the next question. Rajni cannot be sure how much he understood.

qa.q: What did Nitin's mother do that made the questions feel welcome?
qa.a: She said it was a good question, admitted she did not know the sky answer, promised to ask his uncle and kept turning to listen.

qa.q: How might Nitin's mother have felt about the stream of questions on the bus?
qa.a: She was probably a little stretched but kind, since she kept turning to listen and answering honestly.

grounding: A child asks endless why questions; an adult who treats them as worth answering matters more than the answers.

passage: Monday: Five-year-old Ganga asked her father, Omkar, why the moon kept coming along with the car. He slowed down. "Good question. What do you think?" Wednesday: he brought a library book about the moon and looked at the pictures with her. Saturday: Ganga sat with Nani and explained, "The moon is very far, so it seems to follow us!" Nani asked, "Who taught you that?" Ganga said, "We looked it up. I asked."

qa.q: What did Ganga ask her father on Monday?
qa.a: Ganga asked why the moon kept coming along with the car.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling on Saturday as she explained about the moon?
qa.a: Ganga was proud and excited to share what she had found out.

qa.q: What did Omkar do that kept Ganga's curiosity going?
qa.a: Omkar said it was a good question, asked what Ganga thought and then brought a library book to look at together.

qa.q: How might Nani have felt hearing Ganga explain the moon?
qa.a: Nani was probably surprised and pleased, since Nani asked who taught it and heard that Ganga had asked and looked it up.

grounding: A child asks about the moon and the car; an adult treats the question as worth answering across several days.

passage: On the way back from the fields in Chandor, Maria, five, walked beside her big sister Ira. "Why is the sky blue?" Ira thought. "Sunlight has lots of colours, and the blue bounces around the most." "Why is Avó so old?" "Because she's lived a long time. She was little like you once." Maria stopped. "Avó was LITTLE?" "Yes." "Why does the moon come out when it's still day?" Ira laughed. "Good question. I don't know. Let's ask Papa tonight." Maria skipped ahead, already asking the next why.

qa.q: Who was Maria walking beside?
qa.a: Her big sister Ira.

qa.q: How did Maria feel when she learned Avó was once little?
qa.a: She was surprised and amazed, stopping in her tracks.

qa.q: What did Ira get right about answering Maria?
qa.a: She gave simple answers, admitted when she didn't know, and suggested asking Papa, showing the questions were worth answering.

qa.q: How might Ira feel about all the questions?
qa.a: She seems amused and patient, laughing and treating each question seriously.

grounding: Shows a young child asking endless why questions and an older sister treating them as worth answering.

passage: In the back seat on the drive home through Oslo, Ingrid, four, pressed her nose to the window. "Pappa, why is the moon following us?" Hiroshi smiled in the mirror. "Because it's very far away, so it looks like it moves with us." "Why is it far?" "Because space is very big." "Why is space big?" Hiroshi laughed. "That's a very good question. I'm not sure anyone knows. What do you think?" Ingrid thought hard. "Because the moon needs room to play." Hiroshi nodded. "That's a nice idea." Ingrid waved at the moon all the way home.

qa.q: What did Ingrid think was following them?
qa.a: The moon.

qa.q: How did Ingrid seem to feel when Pappa asked what she thought?
qa.a: She seemed pleased and thoughtful, thinking hard and offering her own idea proudly.

qa.q: What did Hiroshi do that kept Ingrid curious?
qa.a: He answered simply, admitted what nobody knows, and asked what she thought, treating her questions as worth answering.

qa.q: What would change if Hiroshi had said 'Stop asking questions'?
qa.a: Ingrid might have felt her wondering was unwelcome and stopped asking.

grounding: Shows a young child asking chains of why questions and a parent treating them as worth answering.

passage: In the clinic waiting room, Mehak, five, sat on Lokesh mama's lap. "Why do people get sick?" "Sometimes tiny germs get into our bodies." "Why are germs tiny?" "Hmm. Maybe so they can hide." "Why is that lady's hair white?" Lokesh mama whispered, "Because she's older. Hair gets white when we get older." "Will my hair be white?" "One day, yes." Mehak thought. "Will yours be white first?" "Yes, first mine." A man nearby smiled. Mehak kept asking why until her name was called, and Lokesh mama answered every one.

qa.q: Where were Mehak and Lokesh mama sitting?
qa.a: In the clinic waiting room.

qa.q: How did Mehak seem to feel asking all those questions?
qa.a: She seemed curious and comfortable, happily asking one why after another on her uncle's lap.

qa.q: What small thing did Lokesh mama do that mattered most?
qa.a: He answered every question patiently, even whispering, showing her questions were welcome.

qa.q: How might the man nearby see Lokesh mama's patience?
qa.a: He seemed amused and warmed, smiling at the gentle back-and-forth.

grounding: Shows a young child asking endless why questions and an adult treating them as worth answering.

passage:
Monday. In the car, Nitin pressed his face to the window. "Why is the moon following us?" Yogesh Chacha laughed. "Good question! It's so far away that it looks like it moves with us."
Wednesday. "Why is Dadi's skin wrinkly?" "Because she has lived a long time, and skin folds as people get older. You could ask her how old she is."
Saturday. "Why is the sky blue?" Chacha scratched his head. "I don't know exactly. Shall we find out tonight?" That night Nitin fell asleep holding the picture book about sunlight.

qa.q: What did Nitin ask on Wednesday?
qa.a: He asked why Dadi's skin is wrinkly.

qa.q: How was Nitin feeling as he asked all these questions?
qa.a: He was curious and eager 🤔 pressing his face to the window and asking something new each day.

qa.q: Why was "I don't know exactly. Shall we find out?" a good answer?
qa.a: It showed Nitin his question was worth answering and turned not knowing into finding out together.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel if Nitin asks her how old she is?
qa.a: She might feel amused and touched that he is curious about her life.

grounding: Shows a young child's stream of why questions and an adult who treats every one of them as worth answering.
